docs.title: How to Learn Python from Scratch
docs.text:
Welcome! This is a free, beginner-friendly guide to mastering Python — written in plain English, packed with examples you can run, and fact-checked against the official Python documentation and the most respected Python books.

No prior programming experience needed. You'll go from "what is Python?" all the way to advanced topics like decorators, generators, and async.

Start with Part 1 :material-arrow-right: See the full roadmap

docs.title: How this course works
docs.text:
• :material-book-open-variant: Read on this website — with search, dark mode, and one-click copy on every code block.
  • :material-rocket-launch: Run it live — open the free Python Playground on Google Colab (no installation needed), paste any example, and press ▶.
  • :material-lightbulb-on: Learn by doing — each lesson explains one idea simply, then shows it with an example you can run and tweak yourself.

The golden rule of learning to code

Don't just read the examples — run them, then change something and see what happens. Breaking things on purpose is the fastest way to understand how they work.

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
1. Getting Started — what Python is, installing it, your first program
  2. Basics — variables, numbers, strings, booleans, input/output
  3. Control Flow — if/else, loops
  4. Data Structures — lists, tuples, dictionaries, sets, comprehensions
  5. Functions — arguments, scope, lambdas, *args/**kwargs
  6. Files & Errors — reading/writing files, exceptions
  7. Object-Oriented Programming — classes, inheritance, dunder methods
  8. Intermediate — modules, the standard library, iterators, generators, decorators
  9. Advanced — type hints, regex, concurrency, testing, performance
  10. Pythonic Practices — PEP 8, idioms, where to go next

See the Roadmap for the full chapter list.

docs.text: Every concept is cross-checked against authoritative references so you can trust what you read: the official Python docs, Python Crash Course (Matthes), Think Python (Downey), Fluent Python (Ramalho), Automate the Boring Stuff (Sweigart), and Real Python.

docs.title: 1. What is Python?
docs.text:
:material-rocket-launch: Run examples in Colab

In one sentence: Python is a programming language — a way to give a computer instructions using text that reads almost like English.

docs.title: Why a "language"?
docs.text:
A computer only understands very low-level signals. A programming language lets you write instructions in a form you can read, which the computer then carries out. Python is famous for being one of the most readable languages — which is exactly why it's the world's most popular first language.

Here's a complete, working Python program:

print("Hello, world!")

When you run it, the computer prints:

Hello, world!

That's it — one readable line. Many other languages need several lines of setup to do the same thing. That readability is Python's superpower.

docs.title: A few facts worth knowing
docs.text:
• Created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991.
  • Named after the comedy group Monty Python — not the snake. 🐍
  • Interpreted: Python runs your code line by line, so you can try things instantly without a separate "compile" step.
  • Dynamically typed: you don't have to declare what kind of value a variable holds — Python figures it out (more on this soon).
  • Free and open source.

Python 2 vs Python 3 — always use Python 3

You may see old tutorials using Python 2. It was officially retired on January 1, 2020 and should not be used. This course uses Python 3 (the current line), which is what everyone uses today.

docs.title: What is Python used for?
docs.text:
Python is a generalist — it shows up almost everywhere:

Area Examples Data science & AI pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch Web development Django, Flask, FastAPI Automation / scripting renaming files, scraping websites, sending emails Anything else games, finance, science, hardware…

Why this matters for you

Because Python is used in so many fields, the time you invest learning it pays off no matter which direction you go — data, web, automation, or AI.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Python is a readable programming language for telling computers what to do.
  • It's interpreted and dynamically typed, which makes it beginner-friendly.
  • Always use Python 3.
  • It's used across data, web, automation, AI, and more.

Source: python.org — About and the official docs.

:material-arrow-right: Next: Install Python & run your first program

docs.title: 2. Install Python & run your first program
docs.text:
:material-rocket-launch: Run examples in Colab

You have two ways to run Python. Pick whichever feels easier — you can switch later.

docs.title: Option A — Zero install (recommended to start)
docs.text: Use the free Python Playground on Colab. It runs Python in your browser — nothing to install. Type code in a cell and press ▶ (or Shift+Enter). This is the fastest way to start today.

docs.title: Option B — Install Python on your computer
docs.text:
When you're ready to run Python locally:

  1. Go to python.org/downloads.
  2. Download the latest Python 3 version for your system.
  3. Run the installer.

Windows users: tick 'Add Python to PATH'

On the first screen of the Windows installer, check the box "Add Python to PATH" before clicking Install. It saves a lot of headaches later.

Check it worked by opening a terminal (Terminal on Mac, Command Prompt on Windows) and typing:

python3 --version

You should see something like Python 3.12.x.

docs.title: Your first program
docs.text:
Let's run the traditional first program every coder writes. In Colab (or a file called hello.py), type:

print("Hello, world!")

Run it. The output is:

Hello, world!

🎉 You just wrote and ran a program! Let's understand it:

  • print(...) is a function — a built-in command that displays whatever you put inside the parentheses.
  • "Hello, world!" is a string — text, which always goes inside quotes.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Change the message and run it again:

print("My name is Tim and I'm learning Python!")

Experiment

What happens if you forget the quotes, like print(Hello)? Try it — you'll get an error. Reading and understanding errors is a real skill you'll build throughout this course, so don't be afraid of them.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The easiest way to start is the Colab Playground (no install).
  • To install locally, get Python 3 from python.org (Windows: Add Python to PATH).
  • print("...") displays text; text goes inside quotes.

docs.title: 3. How to use this course
docs.text:
:material-rocket-launch: Open the Colab Playground

A quick guide to getting the most out of these lessons.

docs.title: The loop that actually works
docs.text:
For every example you see:

  1. Read the explanation.
  2. Run the code (paste it into the Colab Playground and press ▶).
  3. Change something and run it again — predict what will happen first, then check.

Predict, then run

Before you run an example, guess the output in your head. When you're right, it confirms you understand. When you're wrong, you've just found a gap — that's a good thing.

docs.title: Things you'll see in the lessons
docs.text:
Code blocks — copy them with the copy button in the top-right corner:

print("Copy me with the button →")

Expected output is shown like this:

Copy me with the button →

Helpful callouts:

Note

Extra context that's good to know.

Tip

A shortcut or best practice.

Watch out

A common mistake to avoid.

docs.title: How the course is organized
docs.text: We go in order, from the absolute basics to advanced topics. Each part builds on the previous one, so it's best to follow along top to bottom. See the Roadmap for the full list.

docs.title: A note on pace
docs.text: There's no rush. It's far better to truly understand a small thing and be able to use it than to skim ten things. If a concept doesn't click, run the examples a few times and tweak them — it will.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Read → Run → Change, for every example.
  • Predict outputs before running.
  • Go in order; take your time.

:material-arrow-right: Next: Variables & data types

docs.title: 1. Variables & data types
docs.text: :material-rocket-launch: Run examples in Colab

docs.title: What is a variable?
docs.text:
A variable is a name that stores a value so you can use it later. Think of it as a labelled box: you put something in the box and write a name on it.

You create a variable with = (the assignment operator):

name = "Tim"
age = 19

Now name holds "Tim" and age holds 19. Use them anywhere:

print(name)
print(age)

Output:

Tim
19

= means 'store', not 'equals'

age = 19 reads as "put 19 into age." It's an instruction, not a math statement. (To check if two things are equal, you'll later use ==.)

docs.title: Python figures out the type for you
docs.text:
Unlike some languages, you don't declare what kind of value a variable holds — Python knows from what you put in it. This is called dynamic typing. You can even change it:

x = 10        # x is a number
x = "hello"   # now x is text — totally fine

docs.title: The core data types
docs.text:
These five cover almost everything you'll do at first:

Type Name Example int whole number 42, -7, 0 float decimal number 3.14, -0.5 str text ("string") "hello", 'Python' bool true/false True, False NoneType "nothing" None

You can check any value's type with the built-in type() function:

print(type(42))
print(type(3.14))
print(type("hello"))
print(type(True))

Output:

<class 'int'>
<class 'float'>
<class 'str'>
<class 'bool'>

docs.title: Naming variables
docs.text:
Rules (required):

  • Use letters, numbers, and underscores (_) — but can't start with a number.
  • Names are case-sensitive: age and Age are different.
  • Can't use Python's reserved words (like if, for, class).

Convention (strongly recommended):

  • Use lowercase words joined by underscores — called snake_case: first_name, total_price.
first_name = "Tim"     # good ✅
totalPrice = 9.99      # works, but not the Python style
2cool = "nope"         # ERROR ❌ — can't start with a number

Name things clearly

n = 19 works, but age = 19 tells the reader what it means. Good names make your code explain itself.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A variable is a name that stores a value, created with =.
  • Python is dynamically typed — it infers the type, and you can reassign freely.
  • Core types: int, float, str, bool, None. Check with type().
  • Use snake_case and meaningful names.

Source: Python docs — An Informal Introduction.

:material-arrow-right: Next: Numbers & math

docs.title: 2. Numbers & math
docs.text:
:material-rocket-launch: Run examples in Colab

Python has two main number types:

  • int — whole numbers: 42, -7, 1000000
  • float — numbers with a decimal point: 3.14, -0.5, 2.0

docs.title: Arithmetic operators
docs.text:
print(7 + 3)    # addition
print(7 - 3)    # subtraction
print(7 * 3)    # multiplication
print(7 / 3)    # division
print(7 // 3)   # floor division (drops the remainder)
print(7 % 3)    # modulo (the remainder)
print(7 ** 3)   # exponent (7 to the power of 3)

Output:

10
4
21
2.3333333333333335
2
1
343

A few that surprise beginners:

  • / always gives a float, even 6 / 2 is 3.0.
  • // is floor division — it divides and throws away the decimal part: 7 // 3 is 2.
  • % is modulo — the remainder: 7 % 3 is 1. (Great for "is this number even?": n % 2 == 0.)
  • ** is power, not ^.

docs.title: Order of operations
docs.text:
Python follows normal math rules (PEMDAS): ** first, then * / // %, then + -. Use parentheses to be explicit:

print(2 + 3 * 4)      # 14  (multiplication first)
print((2 + 3) * 4)    # 20  (parentheses first)

docs.title: Mixing ints and floats
docs.text:
If you mix them, the result becomes a float:

print(5 + 2.0)   # 7.0
print(type(5 + 2.0))

7.0
<class 'float'>

docs.title: Handy built-in functions
docs.text:
print(abs(-8))        # 8   — absolute value
print(round(3.14159, 2))  # 3.14 — round to 2 decimals
print(max(4, 9, 1))   # 9
print(min(4, 9, 1))   # 1

You can also convert between types:

print(int(3.9))     # 3   — int() chops off the decimal (doesn't round!)
print(float(5))     # 5.0
print(int("42") + 1)  # 43 — turn text "42" into a number

Floats aren't perfectly precise

Try this: 

print(0.1 + 0.2)

0.30000000000000003
That's not a Python bug — it's how all computers store decimals (in binary). For money or exact values, you'll later use the decimal module. For now, just know it can happen.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Two number types: int (whole) and float (decimal).
  • Operators: + - * / and the tricky ones — // (floor), % (remainder), ** (power).
  • / always returns a float; mixing int+float gives a float.
  • Useful tools: abs(), round(), min(), max(), and int()/float() conversion.

Source: Python docs — Numbers.

:material-arrow-right: Next: Strings

docs.title: 3. Strings
docs.text:
:material-rocket-launch: Run examples in Colab

A string (str) is text. You create one by wrapping characters in quotes — single or double, your choice (just be consistent):

greeting = "Hello"
name = 'Tim'

Need a quote inside the text? Use the other kind on the outside:

sentence = "It's a great day"   # single quote inside double quotes

For text spanning multiple lines, use triple quotes:

poem = """Roses are red,
Python is fun."""

docs.title: Joining and repeating
docs.text:
first = "Py"
second = "thon"
print(first + second)   # join with +  -> Python
print("ha" * 3)         # repeat with * -> hahaha

docs.title: f-strings: putting values into text (the modern way)
docs.text:
Put an f before the quotes, then drop variables inside { }. This is the standard, readable way to build text:

name = "Tim"
age = 19
print(f"My name is {name} and I am {age} years old.")

Output:

My name is Tim and I am 19 years old.

Prefer f-strings

f-strings (added in Python 3.6) are clearer and faster than older approaches like + gluing or .format(). Use them.

docs.title: Reaching into a string (indexing & slicing)
docs.text:
Each character has a position (an index) starting at 0. Negative indexes count from the end.

word = "Python"
#       012345
print(word[0])    # P  — first character
print(word[-1])   # n  — last character
print(word[0:3])  # Pyt — characters 0,1,2 (the end index is NOT included)
print(word[2:])   # thon — from index 2 to the end

Slicing stops before the end number

word[0:3] gives characters 0, 1, 2 — not 3. This "up to but not including" rule is everywhere in Python, so it's worth remembering early.

docs.title: Useful string tools
docs.text:
text = "  Hello, World  "

print(len(text))          # 16 — length (including spaces)
print(text.strip())       # "Hello, World" — remove surrounding spaces
print(text.upper())       # "  HELLO, WORLD  "
print(text.lower())       # "  hello, world  "
print("hello".replace("l", "L"))   # heLLo
print("a,b,c".split(","))          # ['a', 'b', 'c']  -> a list
print("Python".startswith("Py"))   # True

Strings can't be changed in place

Strings are immutable — methods like .upper() return a new string and leave the original untouched: 

name = "tim"
name.upper()       # makes "TIM" but throws it away
print(name)        # still "tim"
name = name.upper()  # reassign to actually keep it
print(name)        # TIM

docs.title: Special characters
docs.text:
Inside strings, a backslash starts an "escape": \n is a new line, \t is a tab.

print("Line 1\nLine 2")

Line 1
Line 2

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Strings are text in quotes; triple quotes span multiple lines.
  • Join with +, repeat with *.
  • Use f-strings (f"Hi {name}") to insert values.
  • Index from 0 (and from -1 at the end); slicing is up to but not including the end index.
  • Handy methods: len(), .strip(), .upper()/.lower(), .replace(), .split().
  • Strings are immutable — methods return a new string.

Source: Python docs — Strings and Text Sequence Type.

:material-arrow-right: Next up (coming soon): Booleans & comparisons

docs.title: 4. Booleans & comparisons
docs.text:
:material-rocket-launch: Run examples in Colab

A boolean (bool) has only two possible values: True or False (capitalized). Booleans are how your programs make decisions.

docs.title: Comparisons produce booleans
docs.text:
When you compare two values, you get back True or False:

print(5 > 3)     # True
print(5 == 5)    # True   (== means "is equal to")
print(5 != 3)    # True   (!= means "is not equal to")
print(2 >= 9)    # False

The comparison operators:

Operator Means == equal to != not equal to > < greater / less than >= <= greater-or-equal / less-or-equal

= vs == — the #1 beginner mistake

= assigns a value (x = 5). == compares (x == 5 asks "is x equal to 5?"). Mixing them up is the most common early bug. Assign with one =, compare with two ==.

docs.title: Combining conditions: and, or, not
docs.text:
age = 20
print(age > 18 and age < 65)   # True  — BOTH must be true
print(age < 13 or age > 65)    # False — at least ONE must be true
print(not age > 18)            # False — flips True/False
  • and → True only if both sides are true.
  • or → True if at least one side is true.
  • not → flips the value.

docs.title: Truthiness: values that "count as" True or False
docs.text:
Every value in Python is either "truthy" or "falsy" when used in a condition. The falsy values are the empty/zero/nothing ones:

  • False, None
  • 0 and 0.0
  • "" (empty string), [] (empty list), {} (empty dict)

Everything else is truthy. You can check with bool():

print(bool(0))       # False
print(bool(""))      # False
print(bool("hi"))    # True
print(bool(42))      # True

Why this is handy

Instead of if len(name) > 0: you can simply write if name: — an empty string is falsy, so it reads naturally as "if there is a name."

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A bool is True or False.
  • Comparisons (==, !=, >, <, >=, <=) return booleans.
  • Combine with and, or, not.
  • Empty/zero/None values are falsy; everything else is truthy.
  • Assign with =, compare with ==.

Source: Python docs — Boolean operations and Truth value testing.

:material-arrow-right: Next: Input & output

docs.title: 5. Input & output
docs.text:
:material-rocket-launch: Run examples in Colab

"Output" means showing things to the user; "input" means getting things from the user.

docs.title: Output with print()
docs.text:
You've used print() already. A few extra tricks:

print("Hello", "world")        # multiple values -> Hello world
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")  # change the separator -> a-b-c
print("no newline", end=" ")   # don't go to a new line
print("same line")

Output:

Hello world
a-b-c
no newline same line
  • print puts a space between multiple values by default (change with sep).
  • It ends with a new line by default (change with end).

The cleanest way to mix text and variables is an f-string:

name = "Tim"
score = 95
print(f"{name} scored {score} points.")

Tim scored 95 points.

docs.title: Input with input()
docs.text:
input() pauses the program, shows a prompt, and waits for the user to type something and press Enter:

name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Nice to meet you, {name}!")

If the user types Tim, the output is:

What is your name? Tim
Nice to meet you, Tim!

docs.title: ⚠️ The big gotcha: input is always text
docs.text:
input() always returns a string, even if the user types a number. So this breaks:

age = input("Your age: ")   # user types 20
print(age + 1)              # ERROR: can't add a number to text

Convert it to a number first with int() (or float()):

age = int(input("Your age: "))   # now age is the number 20
print(f"Next year you'll be {age + 1}.")

Your age: 20
Next year you'll be 21.

Remember the pattern

Reading a number from the user is almost always int(input(...)) or float(input(...)).

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• print() shows output; tweak it with sep and end.
  • Use f-strings to mix text and values cleanly.
  • input(prompt) reads what the user types — always as a string.
  • Wrap it in int() / float() when you need a number.

Source: Python docs — input() and print().

:material-arrow-right: Next: Comments & code style

docs.title: 6. Comments & code style
docs.text: :material-rocket-launch: Run examples in Colab

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
A comment is a note in your code that Python ignores. It's for humans — to explain what's going on. Start a comment with #:

# Calculate the total price including 10% tax
price = 50
total = price * 1.10   # 1.10 adds 10%
print(total)

Python runs the code and skips everything after # on that line. Output:

55.0

Comment the why, not the what

Good comments explain why something is done, not restate the obvious. 

x = x + 1          # bad:  "add 1 to x"  (we can see that)
retries = retries + 1   # good: meaningful name often needs no comment at all
The best "comment" is often a clear variable name.

docs.title: Code style: PEP 8
docs.text:
Python has an official style guide called PEP 8. Following it makes your code look professional and easy to read. The essentials:

  • Indentation: use 4 spaces per level (Python uses indentation to group code — it's not optional decoration!).
  • Naming: snake_case for variables and functions (total_price, not TotalPrice).
  • Spaces around operators: x = 5 + 3, not x=5+3.
  • One statement per line, and keep lines reasonably short.
# follows PEP 8 — clean and readable
first_name = "Tim"
age = 19
is_student = True

if is_student and age < 25:
    print(f"{first_name} gets the student discount.")

Indentation actually matters in Python

In many languages, indentation is just for looks. In Python it's part of the syntax — it's how Python knows which lines belong inside an if, a loop, or a function. Wrong indentation is an error. (You'll see this in action in Part 3.)

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Comments start with # and are ignored by Python — they're notes for humans.
  • Comment the why, and prefer clear names over obvious comments.
  • Follow PEP 8: 4-space indents, snake_case, spaces around operators.
  • In Python, indentation is part of the language, not just style.

Source: PEP 8 — Style Guide for Python Code.
